lead: An internal combustion engine (IC engine) burns its fuel inside its own cylinder. The hot gas pushes a piston, and a crank carries the work out to a shaft. Burning the fuel where the work is done removes the boiler and furnace of a steam plant, so the engine is small, light and starts in seconds; that is why it sits in scooters, cars, gensets and pump sets. Engines differ in a handful of independent choices: how the charge is ignited, how many strokes make a cycle, which ideal cycle it follows, how it is cooled, what it burns, how air is supplied and how the cylinders are arranged. This chapter gives the short history of those choices and the labels that follow from them.
prereq: You need nothing earlier in this book; school physics of pressure, volume and the crank is enough.

sections.h3: From steam to the IC engine: the names to remember

blocks.text: In a steam engine, coal burns in a separate furnace and the heat travels through boiler tubes into steam. Much of it escapes up the chimney, and the boiler is heavy. An IC engine puts the flame next to the moving part, so almost all the heat is released in the gas that does the pushing. An engine of this kind is light enough for a two-wheeler.
Examiners ask for the following people and dates, in this order:

items: Étienne Lenoir, 1860: the first IC engine sold in numbers. It burned coal gas, was lit by an electric spark, and did not compress the charge, so its efficiency was only a few per cent.
Alphonse Beau de Rochas, 1862: stated on paper that the charge should be compressed before ignition, in a four-stroke sequence.

Nikolaus Otto, 1876: built the first working four-stroke engine with compression. Almost every petrol engine still follows his sequence of intake, compression, power and exhaust; see four-stroke and two-stroke engines.
Dugald Clerk, about 1880: built a working two-stroke engine, with a separate pump cylinder that filled and swept the working cylinder, giving one power stroke every revolution.
Rudolf Diesel, patent 1892, working engine 1897: compressed air so strongly that it became hot enough to ignite fuel sprayed into it, so no spark was needed.
Felix Wankel, 1950s: the rotary engine, with a triangular rotor in place of a piston.

blocks.text: Compression is the step that made the IC engine efficient: Lenoir had none, Otto and Diesel built their engines round it.

A reciprocating engine has a piston sliding in a cylinder, a connecting rod, and a crank that turns the back-and-forth motion into rotation. Nearly every road vehicle uses this layout, and the rest of this unit is about it. The part names are in engine terminology and components.

A rotary (Wankel) engine has a triangular rotor turning inside a curved housing. Each face of the rotor traps a pocket of gas and carries it through suction, compression, expansion and exhaust in one continuous turn. It is smooth and compact, but sealing the rotor tips against the housing is hard, so few cars use it now.

Classification is several lists, not one. An engine takes one label from each list, and the choices are independent: a two-stroke can be air-cooled or water-cooled, spark-ignited or compression-ignited.

blocks.text: Some syllabi add more bases: the fuel supply (carburettor, port injection, direct injection), the valve location (side valve or overhead valve), the speed (low, medium, high) and the use (automotive, stationary, marine, aircraft). Each is again a separate question.

items: Ignition. In an SI engine a spark plug lights a fuel-air mixture prepared earlier. In a CI engine, fuel is sprayed into air that compression has made hot, and it ignites by itself; see working principle of SI and CI engines.

Strokes. A four-stroke engine needs two crankshaft revolutions per cycle; a two-stroke needs one. Small two-strokes use ports in the cylinder wall; large two-stroke diesels use an exhaust valve in the head with inlet ports in the wall.

Air supply. A naturally aspirated engine fills its cylinder at about atmospheric pressure. A supercharger (driven by the crankshaft) or a turbocharger (driven by an exhaust turbine) pushes in denser air, so more fuel burns in the same swept volume. This is taught with cooling and lubrication, in the unit on supercharging.
Fuel. Petrol, diesel, CNG, LPG and alcohol blends are all in mass production. Hydrogen IC engines are in trials and small-series production; most hydrogen vehicles on the road use fuel cells instead.

blocks.text: Petrol with spark ignition: scooters, motorcycles, cars and small gensets. Petrol mixes with air easily and the spark fixes the moment of burning. Diesel with compression ignition: trucks, buses, tractors and irrigation pump sets, where the engine runs for long hours and fuel cost per kilometre matters. CNG runs city buses and autorickshaws; its high octane rating lets an SI engine use a higher compression ratio.

Two-strokes give one power stroke per turn with few parts, so they are cheap and lively, but some fresh charge escapes with the exhaust. Stricter emission rules moved Indian two-wheelers to four-strokes; two-strokes survive in chainsaws, outboard motors and very large ship engines. Air cooling suits motorcycles and small gensets; water cooling suits cars, trucks and any large engine that must hold a steady temperature under load.

spec.aria: A tree from IC engine to seven classification bases: ignition, strokes, cycle, fuel, cooling, air supply and cylinders, each with its types. SI, two-stroke, Otto, petrol, air, natural and single are highlighted for the scooter.

examples.question: A scooter engine carries these particulars: fuel petrol, spark plug, two-stroke, cooling fins and no radiator, no blower or turbocharger, one cylinder of 150 cm³. (a) Classify it under seven headings. (b) How many power strokes does it make in 1000 revolutions of the crankshaft, and how many would a four-stroke cylinder make?
steps: Ignition: a spark plug lights a prepared mixture, so the engine is spark ignition (SI).
Strokes: stated as two-stroke, so one power stroke per crankshaft revolution.
Cycle: an SI engine adds heat almost at constant volume, so it follows the Otto cycle.
Fuel: petrol. Cooling: fins and no radiator, so air-cooled.
Air supply: no blower or turbocharger, so naturally aspirated. Cylinders: single.
Two-stroke power strokes: 1000 rev × 1 power stroke per rev = 1000 power strokes.
Four-stroke power strokes: one per 2 revolutions, so 1000 ÷ 2 = 500 power strokes.
The 150 cm³ fixes the size only; it changes none of the seven labels.
examples.answer: SI, two-stroke, Otto cycle, petrol, air-cooled, naturally aspirated, single cylinder; 1000 power strokes in 1000 revolutions against 500 for a four-stroke cylinder.

traps: Two-stroke is not two-cylinder. The label counts piston strokes per cycle, not cylinders; a single-cylinder two-stroke is common.
Diesel is a fuel and a cycle name, while compression ignition is a method. An ignition question wants the words SI or CI.
The history order is Lenoir (1860), Beau de Rochas (1862), Otto (1876), Clerk (about 1880), Diesel (1892 to 1897). Putting Diesel before Clerk, or crediting Otto with the two-stroke, loses the mark.
Supercharged and turbocharged both mean forced induction. A turbocharger is driven by exhaust gas; a supercharger is driven by the crankshaft through a belt or gears.
Air-cooled does not mean uncooled: fins, a fan or the rush of air past a moving motorcycle carry the heat away.

quiz.q: Who built the first IC engine sold in numbers, and what fuel did it use?
quiz.a: Étienne Lenoir, 1860. It burned coal gas, was lit by a spark and did not compress the charge.

quiz.q: Define SI and CI engines in one line each.
quiz.a: SI: a spark plug ignites a prepared fuel-air mixture. CI: fuel is sprayed into air heated by compression and ignites by itself.

quiz.q: Why did compressing the charge make Otto’s engine better than Lenoir’s?
quiz.a: Burning starts at a higher pressure and temperature, so the gas expands through a larger pressure ratio and gives more work from the same fuel. Efficiency rose from a few per cent to more than ten per cent.

quiz.q: A genset engine is diesel-fuelled, four-stroke, water-cooled and turbocharged. Classify it under five headings and find the power strokes per cylinder in 2000 revolutions.
quiz.a: CI, four-stroke, diesel fuel, water-cooled, turbocharged. A four-stroke fires once in two revolutions: 2000 ÷ 2 = 1000 power strokes.

quiz.q: A two-wheeler is sold as “150 cm³, four-stroke, air-cooled”. Which labels are missing?
quiz.a: Ignition, fuel, air supply and cycle are not stated. Petrol, SI and Otto are likely but must be confirmed, and forced induction would change the power from the same 150 cm³.

quiz.q: Engine A: petrol, SI, two-stroke, air-cooled, 100 cm³. Engine B: diesel, CI, four-stroke, water-cooled, turbocharged, 3000 cm³. Match each to a scooter and a highway truck, with reasons.
quiz.a: A is the scooter: light, cheap, air cooling suits a moving vehicle, and the two-stroke gives high power per cm³. B is the truck: CI gives torque and fuel economy over long hauls, water cooling holds the temperature under sustained load, and the turbocharger supplies the air for a loaded truck.

quiz.q: Why is it misleading to call a Wankel engine a four-stroke engine?
quiz.a: It has no piston and so no strokes. Each rotor face carries a chamber through four phases in one continuous turn, so the cycle has four phases but no stroke at all.

beyond: Research engines now use more than four strokes: five- and six-stroke designs recover exhaust energy, and split-cycle engines separate compression from expansion into different cylinders. Opposed-piston two-strokes and hydrogen combustion engines are being developed for trucks. Search terms: split-cycle engine, opposed-piston engine, hydrogen internal combustion engine.
